problems.description: Big-bang rewrite: the entire seed codebase (index.ts Express Todo API) was deleted and replaced with a new multi-file project in a single commit. For a greenfield session this may be intended, but it wipes the baseline wholesale rather than layering the new capability, making the change impossible to review incrementally.

SonarQube delta shows +1 bug, +3 smells, and +33 cognitive complexity across 14 new files (~4511 lines) — the rewrite (build.ts, cache.ts) is materially more complex than the seed it replaced with no compensating simplification.

84 naming convention violations (Classes/Interfaces should be PascalCase, Constants should be UPPER_CASE) concentrated in build.ts, cache.ts, and build.test.ts; mechanical convention score of 0.54 confirms the code diverges from repo style conventions.

package-lock.json declares name 'ssg' with gray-matter/marked deps for a different project identity than the todo seed it replaced — project naming/identity mismatch worth confirming against the session brief.
Committing a 3951-line package-lock.json is fine, but it locks in a new toolchain (jest + ts-jest) that was not present in the seed, adding build/dependency surface to a story baseline.

strengths: Added a proper jest.config.js and a real test suite (build.test.ts), which the seed lacked — improving test coverage posture.
Structured the app into multiple modules (build.ts, cache.ts, cli) with committed package-lock for reproducible installs.
Greenfield commit is coherent and self-contained as a session-1 deliverable.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent but oversized greenfield rewrite that discards the seed codebase wholesale and introduces a bug, 33 points of cognitive complexity, and 84 naming-convention violations (mechanical score 0.54) in a single commit.

problems.description: 84 convention violations across new/modified files (build.ts, build.test.ts, cache.ts): classes and interfaces not PascalCase, constants not UPPER_CASE; convention score 0.54 is the weakest dimension of this commit.
Cognitive complexity +39 with only +1 function added per AST diff — new integration code is heavily nested/branchy, which will be hard to test and modify.

Three new runtime deps (chokidar, handlebars, ws) added in a single integration commit; ws is atypical for a static site generator (implies a live-reload server) and handlebars 4.x carries a known prototype-pollution history, expanding the attack surface.
Session-3 'integration' commit bundles file-watching, templating, and websocket concerns at once; a single session boundary mixing three subsystems makes the change hard to bisect.
Duplications rose +2.3% and smells +1 (SonarQube), adding to debt carried forward from prior sessions.

strengths: Commit message matches the story session convention ('[story] Session 3: integration')
Includes a test file (build.test.ts), so the integration surface has some coverage
Lockfile entries are pinned with integrity hashes; no new bugs reported (SonarQube bugs +0)
Change surface is narrow (2 files + lockfile), consistent with a small session scope
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally complete integration session (chokidar/handlebars/ws) dragged down by heavy cognitive complexity (+39) and 84 naming-convention violations, making this commit net-negative on maintainability.

problems.description: buildSiteWithStats (build.ts) duplicates the full engine setup of buildSite instead of sharing a private helper; the two functions now drift independently and the second is only reachable programmatically

Unsound cast engine.lastBuildStats as BuildStats: the field is declared BuildStats | undefined, so callers can observe undefined at runtime while the type asserts a value; build() should return stats as part of its result instead of exposing post-hoc state

New public mutable field lastBuildStats on the SSG class exposes internal state, breaking the existing pattern where build() returns its result; matches the SonarQube cognitive complexity +36 as build() grew into a multi-branch stateful method
Cache manifest (.ssg-cache.json) is written inside outputDir, so the cache is shipped into the built/deployed site output alongside the pages

Convention score 0.54 with 84 SonarQube violations across build.ts, cache.ts and build.test.ts (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE naming, plus +1 bug and +6 smells), indicating the new code does not follow the repo's established naming/typing conventions

Incremental logic intertwines cache load, template hashing and output-dir wipe/keep semantics inside engine.build(), inflating its complexity rather than delegating to the cache module that owns that concern

strengths: Feature is coherent end-to-end: CLI flags, engine support and stats reporting are wired through the existing parseArgs/engine/plugin pipeline
Cache logic is cleanly separated into its own module (src/cache.ts) with a versioned manifest and clear invalidation rules (template hash + per-page source hash)
Cache invalidation strategy (skip on template change, force clean rebuild via --clean) is sound and matches how the SSG already handles output management
commit_reviews.summary: A useful incremental-build feature that fits the engine architecture but lands with duplicated build entry points, an unsound type cast, a new mutable public field, and a low convention score (0.54), making it a net regression to the codebase.

compounding_issues: Session 1 embedded HTML assembly (document()) and index generation directly in buildSite(), forcing Session 2 to move rendering into TemplatePlugin and thread a content/body/context object through the whole pipeline — a mid-size rewrite of working code

Session 2 hand-rolled regex-based Handlebars and EJS engines instead of using real libraries; the fragile engine (limited {{#if}}/{{#each}}, flat partial lookup, Function/with-based EJS) became a permanent constraint carried into later sessions

Session 4's plugin refactor is only partially realized: DevServerPlugin is an empty shell class and Markdown/Template plugins are dispatched via instanceof checks and direct calls rather than uniform hook dispatch, so the core still special-cases built-ins

Because the S4 plugin pipeline is partial, Session 5's incremental cache had to defensively gate render caching behind renderCacheEnabled = !plugins.some(p => p.onFile) and reach into plugin internals rather than using the hook API
Session 4 introduced require() of a TypeScript ssg.config.ts, which only resolves in ts-jest/ts-node environments — a latent runtime fragility for the plain-node CLI
The 'cache parsed frontmatter' requirement in Session 5 was only partially delivered: rendering is cached but parsing re-runs on every change, and parse-level cache reuse is limited
key_decisions: Single buildSite() orchestrator as the stable core entry point (Session 1) that CLI, dev server, and all later plugins funnel through
Hand-rolled regex Handlebars/EJS template engines instead of depending on external libraries (Session 2), keeping deps minimal but the engine custom and fragile
Dev server built as a standalone self-contained module with its own HTTP/WS/chokidar lifecycle (Session 3), later reduced to a plugin shell rather than integrated through hooks

Plugin system with onStart/beforeBuild/afterBuild/onFile/onEnd lifecycle hooks plus ssg.config.ts loading, extracting markdown and templates as built-in plugins while preserving the public API (Session 4)
Incremental builds via a versioned .ssg-cache.json manifest keyed on source + template hashes with stale-file cleanup and render-cache disabling for custom onFile plugins (Session 5)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions, with tests growing from 2 to 6 and coverage expanding from basic markdown rendering to the full template/layout/partial stack, the dev server, and incremental-build correctness. Session 1 was a clean, minimal greenfield; Session 2 added templates cleanly while preserving existing behavior; Session 3 delivered a robustly engineered dev server (path-traversal guard, debounced rebuilds, graceful close) without breaking build; Session 4 was the riskiest and weakest step — the plugin refactor is a partial facade with an empty DevServerPlugin and non-uniform dispatch — but the public API stayed intact; Session 5 recovered strongly by delivering a well-tested incremental cache with correct source/template invalidation, clean builds, and accurate stats, though it had to defensively special-case the incomplete plugin pipeline. Net arc: monotonically more capable and better tested, with a shallow dip in architectural honesty at the refactor step.
story_review.summary: A coherent, well-sequenced five-session build in which every feature composes through a stable buildSite core, with only moderate debt accrued from hand-rolled template engines and a partially-realized plugin refactor that the final incremental-build session worked around successfully.
